course: Petrol and Diesel Engine Fundamentals: 0 to 12 Litres

lessons.title: Lubrication System Components and Flow
lessons.body: The lubrication system in a small petrol or diesel engine (up to 12 litres) has one main job: keep metal parts from touching each other. It does this by pumping oil under pressure to bearings, camshafts, and cylinder walls. The main parts are the oil pan (sump), oil pump, pickup tube, oil filter, and oil galleries (passages drilled into the block and head). In most small engines, the pump is driven by the crankshaft or camshaft. Oil sits in the pan. The pump pulls it through a strainer on the pickup tube. Then it pushes oil through the filter and into the main oil gallery. From there, oil flows to the crankshaft main bearings, then through drilled passages to the connecting rod bearings. A small amount splashes onto cylinder walls and piston pins. The camshaft gets oil from a separate gallery. In overhead valve engines, oil also goes up to the rocker arms through pushrods or an external line. After lubricating, oil drains back to the pan by gravity. A pressure relief valve in the pump prevents too much pressure when the oil is cold. A bypass valve in the filter lets oil skip the filter if it gets clogged, so the engine still gets oil. Typical oil pressure for a small diesel is 2 to 4 bar (30-60 psi) at operating speed. For a petrol engine, 1.5 to 3 bar (20-45 psi). If you see the oil light come on at idle, the pressure is below about 0.5 bar (7 psi) â stop the engine immediately. In Africa, dusty conditions mean you must check the oil level daily and change oil more often. Use a clean rag, not your shirt. The dipstick has marks: keep the level between them. Overfilling causes foaming and leaks. Underfilling causes overheating and rapid wear. Always use the correct viscosity oil for your climate.

lessons.title: Engine Oils: Types, Viscosity, and Additives
lessons.body: Engine oil is not just oil. It is a mix of base oil and additives. Base oil comes from crude oil (mineral) or is made in a lab (synthetic). Mineral oil is cheaper but breaks down faster in heat. Synthetic oil lasts longer and flows better in cold. Semi-synthetic is a blend. For small engines in Africa, a good quality mineral or semi-synthetic is fine if you change it often. The most important number on the bottle is viscosity, like 15W-40 or 10W-30. The first number (15W) means winter rating â how thick it is when cold. Lower numbers flow easier in cold. The second number (40) is thickness at 100Â°C. Higher numbers are thicker when hot. In hot African climates, 15W-40 or 20W-50 is common. In colder highlands, 10W-30 works. Never use a viscosity lower than the manufacturer recommends for hot weather â the oil will be too thin and pressure will drop. Additives do specific jobs: detergents clean sludge, dispersants keep soot suspended, anti-wear agents (like zinc) protect metal, rust inhibitors stop corrosion, and foam suppressors stop bubbles. Diesel oils (API CI-4, CJ-4) have more detergents for soot. Petrol oils (API SN) focus on sludge and wear. Never use a petrol-only oil in a diesel engine. Check the API service category on the bottle â it must meet or exceed what your engine needs. Change oil every 5,000 km for mineral, 10,000 km for synthetic, or every 6 months, whichever comes first. In dusty conditions, cut that in half. Always drain the old oil when the engine is warm â it flows better and carries more dirt out. Replace the filter every oil change. Use a new crush washer on the drain plug. Tighten the plug to the correct torque â usually 25-30 Nm for small engines. Over-tightening strips threads. After filling, run the engine for a minute, check for leaks, then check the level again.

lessons.title: Oil Pumps, Filters, and Coolers
lessons.body: The oil pump is the heart of the lubrication system. Most small engines use a gear pump or a rotor pump. Two gears or rotors mesh and trap oil between their teeth, then force it out under pressure. The pump is driven by the crankshaft, camshaft, or a belt. If the pump wears, pressure drops, especially at idle. You can test pressure by removing the oil pressure switch and screwing in a mechanical gauge. Start the engine and read the gauge. If pressure is below spec, the pump or bearings are worn. The oil filter removes dirt, metal particles, and sludge. Most filters are spin-on canisters. Inside is a paper element with a bypass valve. Change the filter every oil change. Before installing a new filter, wipe the mounting surface clean and put a little fresh oil on the rubber gasket. Tighten by hand only â about 3/4 turn after the gasket touches. Never use a wrench to tighten â it crushes the gasket and causes leaks. Some engines have an oil cooler â a small radiator that cools the oil. It is usually a sandwich plate between the filter and block, or a separate unit with coolant lines. The cooler uses engine coolant to keep oil temperature down. If the cooler leaks, oil and coolant mix â you will see milky oil or oil in the radiator. That means a blown head gasket or cracked cooler. In Africa, oil coolers help in heavy traffic and hot weather. Keep the cooler fins clean â blow them out with compressed air. Never use water, which can bend the fins. If you suspect low oil pressure, first check the oil level and filter. Then check the pressure relief valve â it can stick open. Clean it with carburetor cleaner. If the pump is worn, replace it. On small diesel engines, the oil pump is often part of the front cover â replacing it is a big job. Always use a torque wrench on the pump bolts.

lessons.title: Cooling System Components and Operation
lessons.body: The cooling system keeps the engine at the right temperature â usually 80 to 95Â°C for most small engines. If it runs too hot, metal expands, oil breaks down, and parts seize. If too cold, fuel doesn't burn properly and wear increases. The main parts are the radiator, water pump, thermostat, hoses, fan, and coolant passages in the block and head. The water pump is driven by a belt (or timing belt on some engines). It pulls coolant from the radiator and pushes it into the engine block. The coolant flows around the cylinders and up into the head, absorbing heat. Then it goes back to the radiator through the top hose. The radiator has many small tubes and fins. Air passing through the fins carries heat away. A fan pulls air through the radiator when the vehicle is not moving fast enough. The thermostat is a valve that blocks coolant flow until the engine warms up. When cold, it stays closed, so coolant only circulates inside the engine. When it reaches about 82Â°C, it opens and lets coolant go to the radiator. If the thermostat sticks closed, the engine overheats quickly. If it sticks open, the engine runs cold and wastes fuel. The radiator cap holds pressure â typically 0.9 to 1.2 bar (13-17 psi). Pressure raises the boiling point of coolant, so it can run hotter without boiling. Never open a hot radiator cap â steam and boiling coolant will burn you. Wait until the engine is cold. The overflow bottle catches expanded coolant and returns it when the engine cools. Check the hoses for cracks, soft spots, or leaks. Squeeze them â they should be firm but flexible. Replace any hose that is hard or swollen. The fan belt must have about 10-15 mm of deflection when pushed with your thumb. If it squeals, it is too loose. If it is too tight, it wears out the water pump bearing. In dusty conditions, clean the radiator fins with a soft brush or compressed air. Never use a high-pressure washer â it bends the fins.

lessons.title: Coolants and Antifreeze Mixtures
lessons.body: Coolant is not just water. Water alone boils at 100Â°C and freezes at 0Â°C. It also causes rust and scale. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol or propylene glycol) lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point. It also has additives that stop corrosion, lubricate the water pump, and prevent foaming. The correct mix is usually 50% antifreeze and 50% clean water. That gives protection down to about -37Â°C and up to 106Â°C with a 1 bar cap. In hot African climates, you might think you don't need antifreeze. But you do â for the corrosion protection and higher boiling point. Never use more than 70% antifreeze â it actually reduces cooling efficiency. Never use less than 30% â corrosion protection is too weak. Use distilled or deionised water if possible. Tap water in many African cities has high minerals that form scale inside the radiator. If you must use tap water, use rainwater or filtered water. Never mix different colours or types of antifreeze without checking â some are incompatible and form a gel that blocks the radiator. Most modern coolants are OAT (Organic Acid Technology) â usually orange, red, or pink. Older green coolant is IAT (Inorganic Acid Technology). Do not mix them. If you are unsure, flush the system completely and refill with fresh 50/50 mix. Check coolant level in the overflow bottle when the engine is cold. It should be between MIN and MAX. If it is low, top up with premixed coolant, not plain water. If you constantly need to add coolant, you have a leak. Look for white crust around hoses, radiator, or water pump. A pressure tester can find small leaks. Change coolant every 2 years or 40,000 km. Old coolant becomes acidic and eats head gaskets and radiator cores. When draining, dispose of old coolant properly â it is toxic to animals and humans. Never pour it on the ground.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Overheating and Oil Pressure Issues
lessons.body: Overheating and low oil pressure are the two most common killers of small engines. Learn to diagnose them fast. For overheating, first check the coolant level. If it is low, look for leaks. A common leak is a bad water pump weep hole â a small drip under the pump. Next, check the fan belt â if it is loose or broken, the water pump and fan stop working. Then check the thermostat â if it is stuck closed, the top hose will be cold while the engine is hot. Replace it. Also check the radiator cap â a weak cap lets coolant boil at a lower temperature. Test it with a pressure tester. If the radiator fins are clogged with mud or insects, clean them. If the electric fan does not come on, check the fuse, relay, and temperature sensor. In traffic, if the temperature gauge climbs, turn off the A/C and turn on the heater to full hot â that dumps heat into the cabin and can save the engine. If the engine is already boiling, pull over safely, shut it off, and wait 30 minutes before opening the hood. Never add cold water to a hot engine â the block can crack. For low oil pressure, first check the oil level. If it is full, the oil pressure switch might be bad â replace it. If the light stays on, screw in a mechanical gauge. If pressure is low at idle but rises with RPM, the bearings are worn. If pressure is low at all speeds, the oil pump is worn or the pickup tube is clogged. Remove the pan and clean the pickup screen. If the oil is thin and smells like fuel, you have a fuel dilution problem â a leaking injector or fuel pump. Change the oil and fix the fuel issue. If the oil is milky, coolant is mixing with oil â blown head gasket or cracked block. Stop driving. In Africa, dusty conditions clog oil filters and radiators faster. Check both weekly. Keep spare belts, hoses, and a gallon of premixed coolant in your vehicle. Learn to read your gauges â a sudden change means something is wrong. Act fast to avoid a rebuild.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Engine Lubrication and Cooling

For any African workshop, fleet operator, or agribusiness running diesel gensets, irrigation pumps, pickup trucks, or tractors between 0 and 12 litres, lubrication and cooling are the two systems that most often decide whether a machine earns money or eats it. A seized bearing or a warped cylinder head can put a transport business out of action for weeks and cost more than the engine is worth. This module gives you the practical reference points â components, flow paths, oil and coolant choices, and troubleshooting logic â that you can apply directly in the bay, the field, or the parts counter. Every figure and table here is drawn from manufacturer and standards-body data so you can cross-check before you buy or specify.

1. Lubrication System: Components and Flow

The lubrication system in a 0â12 litre engine has one job: deliver clean, pressurised oil at the correct viscosity to every bearing, piston, and camshaft surface, then return it to the sump to be cooled and filtered again. The main components are the sump, oil pump (gear, rotor, or variable-displacement), pickup tube and strainer, pressure relief valve, full-flow filter, bypass filter (on many African-market diesels), oil cooler, main gallery, and the crankshaft drillings that feed big-end and main bearings. On turbocharged engines, a dedicated feed line supplies the turbocharger bearing housing, and a drain line returns oil to the sump by gravity.

Flow sequence: sump â strainer â pump â relief valve (bypasses excess) â full-flow filter â oil cooler â main gallery â main bearings â crankshaft drillings â big-end bearings â camshaft and valve train â gravity return to sump. Turbo feed branches off the gallery before the main bearings on most engines, which is why a failing turbo can starve the bottom end if the feed line is restricted.

2. Engine Oils: Types, Viscosity, and Additives

API service categories matter more than brand in most African markets. For modern 0â12 litre diesels with EGR or DPF, use API CK-4 or FA-4; for older mechanically injected engines, API CI-4 or CH-4 is acceptable. Viscosity grade must match ambient temperature: SAE 15W-40 is the default for tropical and subtropical Africa, SAE 10W-30 for cooler highland regions, and SAE 5W-40 for cold-start conditions or engines with tight bearing clearances. Additives â detergents, dispersants, anti-wear (ZDDP), friction modifiers, and oxidation inhibitors â are what separate a $4/litre oil from a $12/litre oil. In high-sulphur diesel markets, a high TBN (Total Base Number) oil, typically 10â14 mg KOH/g, is essential to neutralise acid.

Table 1: Typical engine oil viscosity selection by ambient temperature (Africa context)
Ambient temperature range Recommended SAE grade API category (typical) Change interval (hours / km)
> 40 Â°C (Sahel, lowveld) 15W-40 or 20W-50 CI-4, CK-4 250 h / 10,000 km
25â40 Â°C (most of sub-Saharan Africa) 15W-40 CI-4, CK-4 250 h / 10,000 km
10â25 Â°C (highland plateaus) 10W-30 or 15W-40 CK-4 300 h / 12,000 km
< 10 Â°C (cold start, high altitude) 5W-40 CK-4, FA-4 300 h / 12,000 km

Source: Derived from API Engine Oil Licensing and Certification System (API 1509, 21st edition, 2022) and SAE J300 viscosity classification. Intervals assume good filtration and fuel sulphur below 500 ppm; reduce by 30â50% on high-sulphur fuel or dusty conditions.

3. Oil Pumps, Filters, and Coolers

Oil pumps are positive-displacement: gear, rotor, or variable-displacement vane. A worn pump shows up as low hot idle pressure, usually below 1.0 bar (15 psi). The relief valve opens at 4â6 bar on most 0â12 litre engines; if it sticks open, pressure collapses. Filters are rated by micron efficiency and beta ratio â a Î²200 = 75 means 75% of particles â¥ 20 Âµm are captured. In dusty African operating conditions, use a filter with at least Î²200 = 200 (99.5% at 20 Âµm) and never exceed the manufacturer's interval. Oil coolers are either plate-and-fin or tube-and-shell, cooled by engine coolant or air. A clogged cooler raises oil temperature and accelerates oxidation; a leaking cooler mixes oil and coolant, producing the classic milky emulsion.

Table 2: Common lubrication and cooling fault symptoms, causes, and field actions
Symptom Likely cause Field action
Low oil pressure at hot idle Worn pump, diluted oil, faulty gauge Verify with mechanical gauge; change oil and filter; test pump
Oil pressure warning at speed Clogged filter, stuck relief valve, blocked pickup Replace filter; inspect relief valve; clean strainer
Milky oil / emulsion Cooler leak, head gasket, condensation Pressure-test cooler; check head gasket; change oil
Overheating under load Low coolant, bad thermostat, clogged radiator, failed fan Top up; test thermostat; back-flush radiator; check fan clutch
Coolant loss without visible leak Head gasket, EGR cooler, heater core Combustion gas test; pressure test; inspect EGR cooler

Source: Compiled from Caterpillar Lubrication and Cooling Systems Application and Installation Guide (LEBW4971) and Cummins Engine Troubleshooting and Repair Manual, B and C series, 2021 editions.

4. Cooling System: Components and Operation

The cooling system maintains metal temperature between roughly 80 Â°C and 95 Â°C. Components: radiator, pressure cap (typically 0.9â1.1 bar), thermostat (82â88 Â°C), water pump (belt or gear driven), fan and fan clutch or viscous drive, coolant passages in block and head, heater core, and expansion tank. On turbocharged engines, an aftercooler or charge-air cooler sits between turbo and intake manifold. The thermostat controls flow; the cap controls boiling point; the fan controls airflow. In African conditions, dust blocking the radiator fins is the single most common cause of overheating â clean the core with compressed air or low-pressure water every 250 hours.

5. Coolants and Antifreeze Mixtures

Use a 50/50 mix of ethylene glycol (or propylene glycol) and deionised water unless the manufacturer specifies otherwise. This gives freeze protection to about â37 Â°C and boil protection to about 108 Â°C at 1 bar cap pressure. Never use raw borehole water in a modern engine â dissolved minerals scale the radiator and attack aluminium. OAT (Organic Acid Technology) coolants are preferred for long-life intervals (up to 5 years or 12,000 hours); IAT (Inorganic Acid Technology) is cheaper but requires more frequent changes. In Africa, where hard water is common, pre-mixed coolant is worth the premium.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pressurised Cooling System

Never open a radiator cap or expansion tank cap while the engine is hot. The system is pressurised to 0.9â1.1 bar and coolant can be above 100 Â°C; release pressure slowly and only after the engine has cooled. Ethylene glycol is toxic â store away from children, livestock, and water sources, and clean up spills immediately. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling coolant or hot oil. In confined workshops, ensure ventilation; exhaust and hot oil vapours are hazardous.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Check oil level daily with engine off and level ground; top up with the correct SAE grade and API category.
  • Replace full-flow oil filter at every oil change; never reuse a filter or stretch the interval beyond 250 hours.
  • Verify oil pressure with a mechanical gauge if the dash warning is suspect; hot idle should be â¥ 1.0 bar.
  • Inspect the oil cooler and coolant hoses for leaks, chafing, and soft spots every 500 hours.
  • Clean radiator fins and charge-air cooler with compressed air every 250 hours in dusty conditions.
  • Test coolant concentration with a refractometer twice a year; maintain 50/50 mix and correct OAT/IAT type.
  • Check thermostat opening temperature and pressure cap function at every major service.
  • Record oil and coolant consumption trends â rising consumption is an early warning of wear or leaks.

Further Reading

  • API Engine Oil Licensing and Certification System (API 1509) â official service categories and viscosity guidance.
  • SAE J300 â Engine Oil Viscosity Classification â the standard behind every viscosity grade.
  • U.S. Department of Energy â Internal Combustion Engine Basics â free overview of engine systems.
  • Caterpillar Engines â Lubrication and Cooling Application Guides â free technical downloads for diesel engines.
  • Cummins Engines â Troubleshooting and Repair Resources â free service information for B and C series engines.

Business-first takeaway: In African agribusiness, every hour of downtime has a cost. A disciplined lubrication and cooling routine â correct oil, correct filter, clean radiator, tested coolant â is the cheapest insurance you can buy. Budget for it as a line item, not an afterthought, and your engines will return the favour with longer service life and lower cost per hectare or per tonne-kilometre.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the lubrication system?
options: B) Keep metal parts from touching each other
quiz.explanation: Lubrication creates an oil film that separates moving metal parts to reduce wear.

quiz.q: Which component pulls oil from the pan and pushes it through the filter?
quiz.explanation: The oil pump is responsible for circulating oil under pressure.

quiz.q: What does the oil pressure relief valve do?
options: B) Prevents too much pressure when oil is cold
quiz.explanation: The relief valve opens to bypass excess oil and keep pressure within safe limits.

quiz.q: Typical oil pressure for a small diesel engine at operating speed is:
quiz.explanation: Most small diesel engines run 2 to 4 bar (30-60 psi) when warm and running.

quiz.q: What should you do if the oil light comes on at idle?
quiz.explanation: The oil light indicates dangerously low pressure; continuing to run can destroy the engine.

quiz.q: What does the 'W' in 15W-40 mean?
quiz.explanation: The 'W' stands for winter and indicates cold-weather flow characteristics.

quiz.q: Which oil viscosity is commonly used in hot African climates?
quiz.explanation: 15W-40 is thick enough for high temperatures and provides good protection.

quiz.q: What do detergents in engine oil do?
quiz.explanation: Detergents help keep engine internals clean by removing deposits.

quiz.q: Why should you never use a petrol-only oil in a diesel engine?
quiz.explanation: Diesel oils have higher detergent levels and soot dispersants that petrol oils lack.

quiz.q: How often should you change mineral engine oil in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dust accelerates oil contamination, so change more frequently, often half the normal interval.

quiz.q: What should you do before installing a new oil filter?
options: B) Put oil on the rubber gasket
quiz.explanation: A little oil on the gasket ensures a good seal and makes removal easier next time.

quiz.q: What does a bypass valve in an oil filter do?
options: B) Lets oil skip the filter if clogged
quiz.explanation: The bypass valve ensures the engine still gets oil even if the filter is blocked.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an oil cooler?
quiz.explanation: An oil cooler uses coolant or air to reduce oil temperature.

quiz.q: If oil and coolant mix, what will you see?
quiz.explanation: Coolant in oil creates a milky, mayonnaise-like emulsion.

quiz.q: What is the normal operating temperature range for most small engines?
quiz.explanation: Most engines are designed to run between 80 and 95Â°C for efficiency and longevity.

quiz.q: What does the thermostat do?
options: A) Controls coolant flow to the radiator
quiz.explanation: The thermostat blocks or allows coolant flow to maintain proper temperature.

quiz.q: If the thermostat sticks closed, what happens?
quiz.explanation: A closed thermostat prevents coolant from reaching the radiator, causing overheating.

quiz.q: Why should you never open a hot radiator cap?
options: B) Steam and boiling coolant will burn you
quiz.explanation: The system is under pressure; opening it releases scalding steam and coolant.

quiz.q: What is the typical pressure rating of a small engine radiator cap?
quiz.explanation: Most caps hold 0.9 to 1.2 bar (13-17 psi) to raise the boiling point.

quiz.q: How much deflection should a fan belt have?
quiz.explanation: About 10-15 mm of deflection when pushed with a thumb is correct for most belts.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix of antifreeze to water?
quiz.explanation: A 50/50 mix provides the best balance of freeze, boil, and corrosion protection.

quiz.q: Why should you use distilled water in the cooling system?
options: B) It prevents scale and mineral deposits
quiz.explanation: Tap water minerals form scale that blocks radiator tubes and reduces cooling.

quiz.q: What happens if you mix OAT and IAT coolants?
options: B) They form a gel that blocks the radiator
quiz.explanation: Incompatible coolants can react and create a gel, causing overheating.

quiz.q: How often should you change coolant?
quiz.explanation: Coolant additives deplete over time; 2 years or 40,000 km is typical.

quiz.q: What should you check first if the engine overheats?
quiz.explanation: Low coolant is the most common cause of overheating.

quiz.q: What does a cold top hose while the engine is hot indicate?
quiz.explanation: If the top hose is cold, the thermostat is not opening to let hot coolant to the radiator.

quiz.q: If the electric fan does not come on, what should you check?
options: A) Fuse, relay, and temperature sensor
quiz.explanation: The fan circuit includes fuses, relays, and sensors that can fail.

quiz.q: What should you do if the engine is boiling and you need to add coolant?
options: B) Wait 30 minutes, then add slowly
quiz.explanation: Adding cold water to a hot engine can crack the block; wait for it to cool.

quiz.q: If oil pressure is low at idle but rises with RPM, what is likely worn?
quiz.explanation: Worn bearings allow oil to escape more easily at low speeds, dropping pressure.

quiz.q: What should you do if oil smells like fuel?
options: B) Change oil and fix fuel issue
quiz.explanation: Fuel dilution thins oil and reduces lubrication; the fuel leak must be repaired.
